title: Conditions of the Breast
subject: Reproductive System (REPR)

overview.intro: This chapter covers breast disease from benign change and inflammation through benign tumors to carcinoma in women and men. Board questions usually describe a lump, a skin change, or a nipple discharge in a patient of a given age and setting, then ask which lesion it is, whether it raises cancer risk, or what the microscope would show. The unifying ideas are that cancer risk follows epithelial proliferation and atypia, that several benign lesions heal by fibrosis and calcification and so mimic carcinoma, and that the cell of origin (epithelium or stroma) and the adhesion of tumor cells explain how each tumor looks and spreads.
prerequisites: Breast anatomy: lactiferous ducts, terminal duct lobular unit, suspensory (Cooper) ligaments, and axillary lymphatic drainage
Two-layer duct epithelium: luminal cells over myoepithelial cells on a basement membrane
Estrogen and progesterone effects on breast epithelium across the menstrual cycle, pregnancy, and lactation
Types of necrosis, dystrophic calcification, and chronic and granulomatous inflammation
Tumor suppressor genes, cell adhesion molecules, and the steps of invasion and metastasis

connections.how: Hormone exposure drives fibrocystic change, fibroadenoma growth, carcinoma risk, and gynecomastia.
Coagulase and fibrin deposition explain why lactational mastitis tends to localize into an abscess.
Traumatic fat necrosis is the classic nonenzymatic fat necrosis, contrasted with enzymatic fat necrosis in acute pancreatitis.
Germline defects in DNA repair or adhesion, and sex chromosome aneuploidy, explain familial and male breast carcinoma.
Cirrhosis raises the estrogen to androgen ratio and produces gynecomastia.

sections.title: Fibrocystic change and how benign lesions predict cancer risk

blocks.text: Fibrocystic change, also called diffuse cystic mastopathy or fibrocystic breast disease, is the most common benign breast condition. It is not a single disease but a set of changes in the terminal duct lobular unit that reflect repeated cycles of estrogen and progesterone stimulation. It is most common from the 20s to menopause and usually regresses afterward. Patients report lumpy, often bilateral breasts with tenderness that worsens before menstruation, sometimes with a discrete cyst that can be felt.

The organizing principle for board questions is that cancer risk tracks with how much the epithelium proliferates and whether the proliferating cells look atypical. Cysts form when lobules dilate and fill with fluid; large ones can appear blue through the wall and are called blue-dome cysts. Their lining often shows apocrine metaplasia, and ruptured cysts provoke inflammation that heals by fibrosis. These nonproliferative changes involve little epithelial growth and add no meaningful cancer risk.

Proliferative change without atypia includes usual ductal hyperplasia (extra layers of polyclonal cells filling the duct), sclerosing adenosis (increased acini compressed by fibrosis, which can feel firm and calcify), intraductal papilloma, and radial scar. These carry a slightly raised risk because more cell division gives more chances for mutation. Atypical ductal or lobular hyperplasia is a clonal proliferation that shares molecular changes with carcinoma in situ and behaves as a nonobligate precursor and a marker of risk. Its risk applies to both breasts, which shows that it signals a field of susceptible tissue rather than only the spot sampled.

blocks.predict: A biopsy of a tender lump shows a cyst lined by apocrine metaplasia with surrounding fibrosis. How does this change her cancer risk compared with a biopsy showing atypical ductal hyperplasia?

blocks.text: A galactocele is a cyst filled with milk, formed when a lactiferous duct becomes obstructed during lactation or during weaning. The epithelium of the lobule keeps secreting, the outflow is blocked by thickened (inspissated) milk, and the duct behind the block dilates into a smooth, round, usually painless and mobile cyst. It is the most common benign breast mass in lactating women.

The cyst lining is flattened duct epithelium, and the contents are milky fluid rich in fat and protein. Over time the water is resorbed and the fat concentrates, so older galactoceles become thicker and can appear partly solid on imaging. Aspiration yields milky fluid, which both confirms the diagnosis and distinguishes the lesion from a solid tumor.

The key prediction is what happens if the cyst ruptures. Milk lipid and protein are irritants once they leave the duct, so their release into the surrounding stroma triggers an acute and then chronic inflammatory reaction with foamy macrophages and giant cells. The breast becomes locally red, tender, and indurated, and healing by fibrosis can leave a firm nodule. Secondary infection can also occur because stagnant milk is a good culture medium, which links galactocele to acute mastitis.

blocks.text: Mammary duct ectasia is dilation of the large subareolar ducts with stasis of their secretions and chronic inflammation around them. It typically affects women in their 50s and 60s, often multiparous, and, unlike periductal mastitis, it is not specifically linked to smoking. The cause is not certain. The dilated ducts fill with thick, pasty material containing lipid-laden macrophages, and the secretion seeps into the duct wall and surrounding stroma.

That leakage drives a periductal and interstitial chronic inflammatory reaction, sometimes granulomatous, that is characteristically rich in plasma cells. For this reason the older term plasma cell mastitis is sometimes used. The clinical picture follows from the pathology: a poorly defined, firm periareolar mass, thick white or greenish nipple discharge from several ducts, and, less often, pain and redness. The inspissated secretions can calcify, producing calcifications on mammography.

The reason duct ectasia mimics carcinoma is fibrosis. Chronic inflammation heals by collagen deposition, and as scar tissue around the subareolar ducts contracts, it shortens the ducts and pulls the nipple inward. A firm irregular mass, nipple retraction, and calcifications are exactly the features that raise concern for invasive carcinoma, in which desmoplastic stroma also contracts and retracts the nipple. Only tissue examination reliably separates them: duct ectasia shows dilated ducts with plasma cell inflammation and no malignant cells.

blocks.title: Duct ectasia compared with periductal mastitis
rows: Painful red subareolar mass or abscess
blocks.caption: Both are subareolar and both can retract the nipple; the duct lining and the patient profile separate them.

blocks.text: Acute mastitis is bacterial infection of the breast that occurs almost always during breastfeeding, most often in the first weeks to months. Suckling can crack and fissure the nipple, which breaks the skin barrier and lets bacteria from the mother's skin or the infant's mouth enter the ducts. Milk stasis from incomplete emptying or a blocked duct provides a warm, nutrient-rich medium, so the organisms multiply in the ducts and spread into the lobules and stroma.

Staphylococcus aureus is the usual cause. Its coagulase activates prothrombin to convert fibrinogen to fibrin, and together with tissue destruction by its toxins and the neutrophil response, this tends to wall the infection off into a localized collection of pus, a breast abscess. Streptococci, by contrast, secrete enzymes such as hyaluronidase and streptokinase that favor diffuse spread through tissue, so streptococcal infection tends to cause a spreading cellulitis rather than a single abscess.

The manifestations follow from acute inflammation. Vasodilation and increased permeability make the affected segment red, warm, swollen, and painful, and cytokines such as IL-1, IL-6, and TNF reset the hypothalamic set point to produce fever, often 38.5 °C (101.3 °F) or higher, with malaise and leukocytosis. A fluctuant, tender mass that persists within the inflamed area indicates an abscess. Infection is usually unilateral and wedge-shaped, following the segment drained by one duct system.

blocks.text: Periductal mastitis, also called recurrent subareolar abscess or squamous metaplasia of lactiferous ducts, is an inflammatory condition that is not related to lactation. More than 90% of affected patients smoke, and it can occur in women of any adult age and occasionally in men. Smoking is thought to alter the differentiation of the ductal epithelium, possibly through toxic components of smoke or relative vitamin A deficiency, although the exact mechanism is uncertain.

Normally only the most distal portion of each lactiferous duct, at the nipple opening, is lined by keratinizing squamous epithelium. In periductal mastitis, squamous metaplasia extends deeper into the ducts beneath the nipple. The metaplastic cells shed keratin, which accumulates and plugs the duct. The plugged duct dilates and eventually ruptures, spilling keratin into the periductal stroma. Keratin is a powerful irritant outside the epithelium, and it provokes an intense acute and then chronic granulomatous inflammatory response, often with secondary bacterial infection.

The result is a painful, red subareolar mass that may form an abscess. Because the process can recur and may drain through the skin, a fistulous tract can form that opens at the edge of the areola. Inflammation and fibrosis around the ducts can also invert the nipple. The patient is not breastfeeding, which separates this lesion from acute lactational mastitis.

blocks.text: Traumatic fat necrosis is death of breast adipocytes caused by physical injury, including blunt trauma (such as a seatbelt injury), prior surgery, biopsy, or radiation. A clear history of injury is absent in many patients because the trauma may have been minor and forgotten. It is called nonenzymatic to contrast it with the enzymatic fat necrosis of acute pancreatitis, in which released lipase digests fat. In the breast, adipocytes rupture from mechanical or ischemic injury rather than from enzyme attack.

The microscopic picture evolves in a predictable order. Early on there is hemorrhage and necrotic fat with neutrophils. The released lipid is then taken up by macrophages, which become foamy (lipid-laden), and multinucleated foreign body giant cells form around lipid droplets and cholesterol clefts. Over weeks, fibroblasts lay down collagen, hemosiderin marks the old hemorrhage, and dystrophic calcification deposits in the necrotic tissue. Liquefied fat may collect into an oil cyst.

These healing changes explain the clinical problem. The lesion becomes a firm, sometimes irregular, painless mass, and fibrosis can tether it to the skin, causing skin thickening or retraction. On mammography the calcifications and spiculated density can resemble those of carcinoma. Fat necrosis therefore mimics cancer on both physical examination and imaging, and biopsy showing foamy macrophages, giant cells, and fibrosis without malignant cells settles the question.

blocks.caption: Fibrosis and calcification in the late stage are what make fat necrosis mimic carcinoma.

blocks.text: Fibroadenoma is the most common benign tumor of the breast and the most common breast mass in women under about 30. It presents as a small (often 1 to 3 cm), round, rubbery, well-circumscribed mass that moves freely under the fingers because it pushes surrounding tissue aside rather than invading it. Most are solitary, though some women have several, in one or both breasts.

Fibroadenoma is a biphasic tumor arising from the intralobular stroma of the terminal duct lobular unit. The stromal cells are the neoplastic component, and many carry mutations in MED12, a gene involved in transcriptional regulation. The ducts are not neoplastic; they are carried along and may be compressed into slit-like spaces by the expanding stroma. The duct epithelium keeps its normal two-cell layer of luminal and myoepithelial cells, which helps confirm a benign lesion.

Both stroma and epithelium respond to hormones. Fibroadenomas may enlarge late in the menstrual cycle, grow during pregnancy under high estrogen and progesterone, and can show lactational change in the epithelium. After menopause, as estrogen falls, they regress, and the stroma often becomes hyalinized and calcified, producing coarse calcifications on mammography in older women. Fibroadenoma adds little or no cancer risk, although complex fibroadenomas containing cysts, sclerosing adenosis, or calcifications sit in the proliferative without atypia group.

Phyllodes tumor is also a biphasic tumor of intralobular stroma, so it is a relative of fibroadenoma, but its stroma is more cellular, grows faster, and behaves less predictably. It is much less common than fibroadenoma and usually appears in women in their 40s to 60s, roughly 10 to 20 years later than fibroadenoma. The typical presentation is a palpable mass that is often larger and may grow quickly.

The name comes from the Greek for leaf. The hypercellular stroma overgrows the epithelium and pushes into epithelium-lined clefts, producing leaf-like projections when the tumor is cut. Under the microscope the stroma shows more cells than a fibroadenoma, and higher-grade tumors add nuclear atypia, frequent mitoses, stromal overgrowth (stroma without epithelium over a wide field), and infiltrative borders. These features are used to grade tumors as benign, borderline, or malignant.

Because the neoplasm is a stromal (mesenchymal) proliferation, its behavior follows sarcoma rules rather than carcinoma rules. Low-grade tumors may recur locally if incompletely removed, and high-grade tumors can metastasize, chiefly through the blood to the lungs and bone. Spread to axillary lymph nodes is uncommon, which contrasts with breast carcinoma.

blocks.text: An intraductal papilloma is a benign papillary growth inside a duct. The common central (large duct) form is usually solitary and lies in a lactiferous sinus or large duct beneath the areola, typically in women of reproductive age through middle age. Each papilla has a branching fibrovascular core covered by the normal two cell layers, luminal epithelium on the inside and myoepithelial cells beneath. The intact myoepithelial layer is the key feature that separates a benign papilloma from papillary carcinoma, in which the myoepithelial layer is absent within the papillae.

The fronds are delicate and carry small blood vessels. Twisting, infarction, or minor trauma of a frond inside a confined duct bleeds into the lumen, and because the duct opens on the nipple, the blood appears as a serous or bloody discharge from a single duct of one breast. A small subareolar mass may also be felt. Intraductal papilloma is the most common cause of bloody nipple discharge in a woman without a palpable mass. It sits in the proliferative without atypia group, with a slightly raised cancer risk, while multiple peripheral papillomas carry somewhat more risk.

Nipple discharge is interpreted by its color, laterality, and number of ducts, because each pattern points to a different mechanism, as the table shows. Bloody, spontaneous, single-duct discharge is the pattern that most needs explanation, since carcinoma (often DCIS with a papillary pattern) can also produce it, especially in older women.

blocks.text: Breast carcinoma is the most common non-skin cancer in women. Most cases arise in the terminal duct lobular unit, and most are hormone dependent. The risk factors make sense once one principle is clear: each menstrual cycle exposes breast epithelium to estrogen and progesterone, which stimulate proliferation, and every round of proliferation gives another chance for DNA replication errors to be copied and kept. More cycles and more total estrogen therefore mean more accumulated mutations.

Early menarche and late menopause lengthen the span of cycling. Nulliparity and a late first full-term pregnancy increase risk because a full-term pregnancy drives the lobular epithelium to final differentiation, after which it is less responsive to proliferative signals; the earlier this happens, the fewer undifferentiated cycles occur before it. Breastfeeding also lowers risk by suppressing cycling. After menopause the ovary stops making estrogen, and the main source becomes aromatase in adipose tissue, which converts androstenedione to estrone, so postmenopausal obesity raises circulating estrogen and risk.

Age is the strongest single risk factor after female sex; carcinoma is rare before 25 and incidence rises steadily thereafter. Atypical hyperplasia raises risk about 4 to 5 times. Family history matters most when first-degree relatives were affected young or in both breasts, and a minority of cases arise from germline mutations, chiefly BRCA1 and BRCA2, which impair homologous recombination repair of double-strand DNA breaks. Other factors include chest radiation in youth, dense breast tissue, and alcohol use.

About half of carcinomas arise in the upper outer quadrant, simply because that quadrant, with the axillary tail, contains the most glandular tissue. This location also places the tumor close to the axillary lymph nodes, the main drainage route and first site of spread.

blocks.title: Risk factors grouped by mechanism
rows: Early menarche, late menopause, nulliparity, late first pregnancy, postmenopausal obesity

blocks.caption: Most risk factors either add proliferative cycles under estrogen or reduce the ability to repair DNA.

blocks.title: Ranking estrogen-related risk
blocks.text: Two 55-year-old women are compared. Woman A had menarche at 15, a first full-term pregnancy at 22, breastfed three children, and has a BMI of 23 kg/m2. Woman B had menarche at 11, no pregnancies, and a BMI of 34 kg/m2. Step 1: count cycling time; B began cycling 4 years earlier and never had pregnancy or lactation to interrupt it. Step 2: consider differentiation; A's early full-term pregnancy matured her lobular epithelium decades ago, while B's epithelium remains less differentiated. Step 3: consider current estrogen; after menopause, B's larger adipose mass converts more androstenedione to estrone through aromatase. Every factor points the same way, so B has the higher estrogen-related risk, although family history and biopsy findings could still change the overall ranking.

sections.title: Ductal carcinoma in situ and invasive ductal carcinoma

blocks.text: Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) is a clonal proliferation of malignant epithelial cells within ducts and lobules that has not crossed the basement membrane. Because the myoepithelial layer and basement membrane remain intact, the cells have no access to stromal lymphatics or blood vessels, so DCIS cannot metastasize. It is usually not palpable and is most often found on screening mammography as microcalcifications. The calcifications form in two ways: in necrotic debris and in secretions within the duct lumens.

DCIS has several architectural patterns (solid, cribriform, papillary, micropapillary). The comedo type is high grade, with large pleomorphic nuclei; the central cells outgrow their diffusion-dependent blood supply, which lies outside the basement membrane, and die. The necrotic center calcifies, giving linear or branching calcifications on mammography, and on cut section the necrotic material can be squeezed out like a comedone. DCIS is a nonobligate precursor of invasive carcinoma in the same breast, and it can also spread along ducts to the nipple skin as Paget disease.

Invasive ductal carcinoma, also called invasive carcinoma of no special type, accounts for most invasive breast cancers, roughly 70% to 80%. Tumor cells breach the basement membrane and infiltrate stroma as nests, cords, and glands, and they provoke desmoplasia. This dense reactive collagen makes the tumor rock hard with an irregular stellate outline and gritty cut surface, and its contraction pulls on Cooper ligaments to dimple the skin or retract the nipple. Spread is first to axillary lymph nodes, then by blood to bone, lung, liver, and brain. Size, nodal status, grade, and the expression of estrogen and progesterone receptors and HER2 determine behavior.

sections.title: Lobular carcinoma and loss of E-cadherin

blocks.text: Lobular neoplasia is defined by a single molecular event: loss of E-cadherin, the calcium-dependent adhesion protein of adherens junctions encoded by CDH1. Normally E-cadherin molecules on neighboring epithelial cells bind each other and anchor to the actin cytoskeleton through catenins, holding cells in cohesive sheets. In lobular lesions, one CDH1 allele is lost and the other is inactivated by mutation or silencing, so the cells lose their attachment to one another and become discohesive.

Lobular carcinoma in situ (LCIS) is a uniform population of small, round, discohesive cells filling and expanding the acini of a lobule. It rarely forms a mass or calcifications, so it is usually an incidental biopsy finding. It is both a marker of risk and a nonobligate precursor, and the increased risk applies to both breasts. Invasive lobular carcinoma, about 10% of invasive cancers, shows how the lack of adhesion changes the pattern of invasion: cells infiltrate stroma one by one, lined up in single-file strands between collagen bundles, and may encircle normal ducts in a target-like pattern. Some cells contain intracytoplasmic mucin and look like signet ring cells.

Because the cells slip singly through tissue with little desmoplasia, invasive lobular carcinoma often forms a vague thickening rather than a discrete hard mass and can be subtle on mammography. Disease is frequently multifocal in one breast and is bilateral more often than ductal carcinoma. Most tumors are estrogen receptor positive and HER2 negative. Lobular carcinoma also spreads to unusual sites, including the peritoneum, retroperitoneum, leptomeninges, gastrointestinal tract, and ovaries. Germline CDH1 mutation causes hereditary diffuse gastric cancer and raises the risk of lobular breast carcinoma.

blocks.explain: Without cell to cell adhesion the cells invade singly in single-file lines with little desmoplasia, so the tumor forms an ill-defined thickening rather than a hard spiculated mass.

blocks.text: Paget disease of the breast (Paget disease of the nipple) is an uncommon presentation of breast carcinoma, roughly 1% to 4% of cases, in which malignant cells involve the epidermis of the nipple and areola. It presents as a unilateral red, scaly, crusted, eczema-like rash on the nipple that may itch, ooze, bleed, or ulcerate and then spread to the areola. Because it looks like dermatitis, it can be overlooked, which is why a persistent one-sided nipple rash is significant.

The mechanism is intraepithelial spread. Carcinoma cells from an underlying DCIS travel along the lactiferous ducts to the nipple and then move into the squamous epidermis, without crossing the epidermal basement membrane. Their presence separates the keratinocytes and disrupts the epidermal barrier, so fluid exudes and dries into crust. Under the microscope, Paget cells are large, with abundant pale to clear cytoplasm, large nuclei, and prominent nucleoli, scattered singly or in clusters among keratinocytes. They are epithelial cells, so they stain for cytokeratins, and some contain mucin; most overexpress HER2.

Paget disease is nearly always accompanied by an underlying carcinoma in the same breast, either DCIS alone or invasive carcinoma, and a palpable mass usually means an invasive component. Prognosis depends on that underlying tumor rather than on the skin change itself. Two distinctions are commonly tested: eczema is usually bilateral and lacks Paget cells, and melanoma in situ contains melanocytic cells that stain for melanocytic markers (such as S100 and melan-A) rather than cytokeratins. Extramammary Paget disease of the vulva is related in appearance but, unlike the breast form, usually has no underlying carcinoma.

sections.title: Inflammatory carcinoma compared with acute mastitis

blocks.text: Inflammatory breast carcinoma is a clinical presentation, not a separate histologic type; the underlying tumor is usually a high-grade invasive ductal carcinoma. It accounts for only a few percent of breast cancers but has a poor prognosis, and many patients already have distant metastases at diagnosis. Despite the name, the redness and swelling are not caused primarily by inflammation.

The characteristic lesion is tumor emboli within dermal lymphatics. Clumps of carcinoma cells plug the small lymphatic channels in the skin, lymph cannot drain, and the dermis fills with edema fluid. Dilated superficial vessels and congestion give a red, warm appearance over a third or more of the breast. The swollen skin bulges between points where it is tethered to underlying tissue at hair follicles and gland openings, so those points become pits and the surface looks like orange peel (peau d'orange). The whole breast becomes enlarged, firm, and heavy, and there is often no discrete palpable mass because the tumor diffusely infiltrates rather than forming one lump. Onset is rapid, usually over weeks to a few months.

blocks.title: Reading a red breast
blocks.text: A 52-year-old woman who is not breastfeeding has a red, warm, swollen left breast that has enlarged over six weeks. Her temperature is 36.8 °C (98.2 °F), and the skin is thickened and pitted. Step 1: setting; mastitis is a disease of lactation, and she is not lactating. Step 2: systemic signs; infection severe enough to redden a third of the breast should produce fever and leukocytosis, and she has neither. Step 3: skin change; pitting over a broad area means dermal lymphedema, which follows lymphatic obstruction. Step 4: tie the findings to one lesion; tumor emboli in dermal lymphatics explain the redness, edema, and peau d'orange together. Biopsy is expected to show carcinoma, classically within dermal lymphatic channels.

The male breast contains a few ducts embedded in stroma and fat, with no lobules. Estrogen stimulates ductal epithelium and periductal stroma to grow, while androgens oppose this growth, so the balance between the two decides whether the male breast enlarges. Gynecomastia is benign enlargement caused by a raised estrogen to androgen ratio. It forms a firm, rubbery, sometimes tender, disc-like enlargement centered beneath the areola, often bilateral but sometimes one-sided. Histologically, the ducts show epithelial hyperplasia within loose, then later dense, collagenous stroma; lobules usually do not form.

Physiologic gynecomastia occurs in newborns (maternal estrogen), at puberty (estrogen production rises before testosterone reaches adult levels), and in older men (falling testosterone and more adipose aromatase). Pathologic causes act on the same ratio. In cirrhosis, the liver clears estrogens and androstenedione poorly, and more androstenedione is converted to estrogen in peripheral fat. In Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY), damaged testes produce little testosterone, and high LH stimulates aromatase activity. Testicular tumors can secrete estrogen (Leydig cell tumors) or hCG (some germ cell tumors), which drives estrogen production. Drugs act through the same balance, for example spironolactone by blocking androgen receptors.

Male breast carcinoma is rare, about 1% of breast cancers, and usually occurs in older men. It presents as a firm, painless, usually unilateral mass that is often eccentric rather than symmetric beneath the areola and may cause nipple retraction, discharge, or ulceration. Because the male breast is small, tumors reach the skin and chest wall early. Most are invasive ductal carcinomas that express estrogen receptors. The strongest genetic risk factor is a germline BRCA2 mutation, and Klinefelter syndrome raises risk substantially through long-standing high estrogen relative to androgen. Gynecomastia itself is not considered a precursor.

blocks.title: Gynecomastia versus male breast carcinoma
rows: Puberty, cirrhosis, Klinefelter, testicular tumors, drugs
blocks.caption: Symmetric soft enlargement suggests hormone imbalance; a hard eccentric fixed mass suggests carcinoma.

integration.text: Anatomy and physiology set the stage. Nearly all lesions arise in the terminal duct lobular unit or the large subareolar ducts, and location predicts presentation: subareolar disease (duct ectasia, periductal mastitis, papilloma, Paget disease) shows up as nipple discharge, retraction, or skin change, while lobular lesions present as masses or calcifications. Estrogen and progesterone drive normal cyclic proliferation, so the same hormones explain fibrocystic change, fibroadenoma growth, carcinoma risk, and, in men, gynecomastia. Cooper ligaments and axillary drainage explain skin dimpling and the first site of metastasis.

Pathology supplies two reasoning rules. First, risk follows proliferation and atypia, and invasion requires breaching the basement membrane, which the myoepithelial layer helps mark. Second, many benign processes (fat necrosis, duct ectasia, sclerosing adenosis, periductal mastitis) heal by fibrosis and calcification and so reproduce the hardness, retraction, and calcification of carcinoma; only histology settles the difference. Microbiology explains the abscess tendency of S. aureus, and genetics explains why BRCA2 and Klinefelter syndrome dominate male disease and why CDH1 loss produces both lobular breast and diffuse gastric carcinoma.

summary: Benign breast lesions raise cancer risk in proportion to epithelial proliferation and atypia: nonproliferative none, proliferative without atypia about 1.5 to 2 times, atypical hyperplasia about 4 to 5 times, in either breast.
Galactocele is a milk-filled duct cyst of lactation or weaning; rupture releases milk lipid and causes local inflammation.
Duct ectasia (older multiparous women) and periductal mastitis (smokers, keratin plugging from squamous metaplasia) are subareolar inflammatory lesions that can retract the nipple.
Acute mastitis is S. aureus infection through cracked nipples during breastfeeding, with a red, warm, painful breast, fever, and possible abscess.
Traumatic fat necrosis heals with foamy macrophages, giant cells, fibrosis, and calcification, so it mimics carcinoma on exam and mammography.
Fibroadenoma (young women, mobile, hormone responsive) and phyllodes tumor (older women, hypercellular leaf-like stroma, can recur or metastasize) are both stromal biphasic tumors.
Intraductal papilloma is the most common cause of bloody single-duct nipple discharge; its preserved myoepithelial layer marks it as benign.
Carcinoma risk rises with age, cumulative estrogen exposure, atypical hyperplasia, and family history; about half arise in the upper outer quadrant.

DCIS is confined by basement membrane and shows calcifications and comedo necrosis; invasive ductal carcinoma is a hard stellate desmoplastic mass; lobular carcinoma loses E-cadherin and invades in single file, often bilaterally.

Paget disease is intraepidermal spread from an underlying carcinoma; inflammatory carcinoma is tumor in dermal lymphatics causing peau d'orange; male carcinoma links to BRCA2 and Klinefelter syndrome, unlike hormone-driven gynecomastia.

verify: Relative risk values for benign breast lesions (about 1.5 to 2 for proliferative without atypia, about 4 to 5 for atypical hyperplasia, about 8 to 10 for carcinoma in situ) vary slightly between sources; confirm the figures NABNE expects.
The share of periductal mastitis patients who smoke (over 90%) is from Robbins; other series give lower figures.
Percentages for invasive ductal (about 70% to 80%), invasive lobular (about 10%), Paget disease (about 1% to 4%), and male breast carcinoma (about 1%) differ between editions and registries.
The fever threshold given for mastitis (38.5 °C (101.3 °F) or higher) is a common clinical figure, not a fixed criterion; confirm whether NABNE tests a value.
The frequency of bilateral disease in lobular carcinoma and the magnitude of male breast cancer risk in Klinefelter syndrome vary widely by study; this chapter gives no fixed numbers.

Tumor emboli in dermal lymphatics are characteristic of inflammatory carcinoma, but staging criteria define it clinically (erythema and edema of a third or more of the breast) and do not require them on biopsy; confirm the emphasis NABNE expects.
Confirm whether NABNE expects the eponym Zuska disease for periductal mastitis; this chapter uses the descriptive name and mentions plasma cell mastitis only as an older term for duct ectasia.
